items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22C: Safeguards for automated decision-making
items.why: Source of the quotation. The duty applies only to significant decisions based solely on automated processing and at least partly on personal data. Inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, s.80; in force 5 February 2026. Article 22D(3) lets the Secretary of State add to the safeguards by regulation; none were found on legislation.gov.uk on the date checked.
items.quote: provide the data subject with information about decisions described in paragraph 1 taken in relation to the data subject

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 13: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject
items.why: The privacy-notice duty: the existence of automated decision-making subject to Article 22C, with meaningful information about the logic and consequences, given when the data are obtained. Article 14(2)(g) says the same for data obtained elsewhere; Article 12(1) requires clear and plain language.
items.quote: meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject

items.title: Automated decision-making, including profiling: What are the ADM safeguards?
items.locator: Section 'What 'information about decisions' do we have to provide?'
items.why: Consultation draft (updated 31 March 2026), not final guidance. Says the information must be about the actual decision, not a repeat of the privacy notice, and that the routes to challenge should be explained when the decision is given.
items.quote: You must explain how they can do this. You should do this at the point you provide the decision.

items.title: Recruitment rewired: Transparency and safeguards
items.locator: Sections 'Our findings about transparency and safeguards' and 'Discussion'
items.why: What the regulator found in practice: privacy notices that did not clearly mention automated decisions, employers treating the notice as satisfying the safeguard, and candidates given nothing about their own decision. Recruitment only.
items.quote: did not recognise that this was separate to the transparency safeguard within the ADM provisions

items.title: Recruitment rewired: Introduction
items.locator: Section 'How we've examined automated recruitment practices'
items.why: Source of the figure: 37 employers contacted, 16 judged likely to be making automated decisions; all 16 agreed to act. The report's summary page says 'over 30 employers'; this section is the more precise.
items.quote: we determined that 16 employers were likely to be using ADM to make decisions about candidates

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.why: The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page). Deployers of Annex III high-risk systems that make or assist decisions about people must inform them. The page carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus and the text is not yet updated; no application date is given in the brief for that reason.
items.quote: shall inform the natural persons that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 12: Transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of the rights of the data subject
items.quote: in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language
items.why: The plain-language rule. As amended on 5 February 2026 it covers communications made under Articles 15 to 22D, so it reaches information given under the automated decision-making safeguards as well as the privacy notice. It sets a standard of form; it does not say what the notice must contain.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 50C: Safeguards for automated decision-making
items.quote: provide the data subject with information about decisions described in subsection (1) taken in relation to the data subject
items.why: The same duty to tell the person, for law enforcement processing by competent authorities (Part 3 of the Act), which the UK GDPR does not cover. Substituted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80(3); fully in force 5 February 2026. Unlike the UK GDPR version it allows exemptions (for example to avoid prejudicing an investigation) if the decision is reconsidered with meaningful human involvement.

items.title: Automated decision-making, including profiling: What rights do people have?
items.locator: Sections 'What do we need to tell people under the ADM safeguards?' and 'How should we deliver the information?'
items.quote: You should take steps to assess whether the information may confuse people.
items.why: The regulator's draft sets three moments for telling people (on collection, on request, and proactively when a decision is made) and expects the wording to be checked for whether people understand it. Consultation draft updated 31 March 2026, not final guidance; wording may change.

items.title: AI tools in recruitment: Audit outcomes report
items.locator: Executive summary, 'Recommendation: Transparency and explainability', PDF p.7
items.quote: Recruiters must ensure that they inform their candidates how they will process their personal information by AI.
items.why: From the regulator's consensual audits of AI recruitment tool providers (August 2023 to May 2024): recruiters must tell candidates how AI processes their information, and contracts must say which party gives candidates that information. Dated November 2024, before the 2025 Act changed the law; recruitment only; organisations that agreed to be audited.

items.title: Guidelines on Automated individual decision-making and Profiling for the purposes of Regulation 2016/679 (WP251rev.01)
items.locator: Chapter IV, section E 'Right to be informed', PDF p.25
items.quote: tell the data subject that they are engaging in this type of activity
items.why: The European regulators' reading of the notice duty: say the decision-making is happening, give meaningful information on the logic, and explain the consequences; good practice even outside the strict legal trigger. Written on the old Article 22, which the UK replaced in 2026; EU guidance, not binding in the UK.

items.title: Ethics, Transparency and Accountability Framework for Automated Decision-Making
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation, Cabinet Office and Office for Artificial Intelligence
items.locator: Point 5, 'Help users and citizens understand how it impacts them'
items.quote: notifying citizens when a process or service has automated decision-making with plain English explanations
items.why: Government's own standard for departments: notification as the default, in plain English, with exceptions agreed by lawyers and a minister. Applies to government departments only; the date is the page's 'updated' date and the text still cites the old Article 22.

items.title: OECD AI Principles: Transparency and explainability (Principle 1.3)
items.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
items.quote: to make stakeholders aware of their interactions with AI systems, including in the workplace
items.why: International comparator: the intergovernmental principle asks organisations to make people aware and to give those adversely affected enough information to challenge the outcome. Non-binding; broader than the UK duty (not limited to solely automated decisions). The page shows no date; the year given is that of the OECD's latest revision of the principles and was not confirmed on this page.

items.title: 'It's Reducing a Human Being to a Percentage'; Perceptions of Justice in Algorithmic Decisions
items.publisher: Reuben Binns and others (arXiv; published in Proceedings of CHI 2018)
items.quote: Our results suggests there may be no 'best' approach to explaining algorithmic decisions
items.why: Three experimental studies of how people judge the fairness of automated decisions about loans, insurance and CV filtering, by style of explanation. Supports testing notices with real readers and not assuming one format works. Authors' repository copy of a peer-reviewed conference paper; hypothetical scenarios, and the abstract gives no sample size.

items.title: Counterfactual Explanations without Opening the Black Box: Automated Decisions and the GDPR
items.publisher: Sandra Wachter, Brent Mittelstadt and Chris Russell (arXiv; published in Harvard Journal of Law & Technology, 2018)
items.quote: explanations can, in principle, be offered without opening the black box
items.why: Argues a notice can be useful without exposing the model, and sets three aims for it: help the person understand why the decision was reached, give grounds to contest it, and show what could be changed (the 'counterfactual' form of explanation the title names). Authors' repository copy (v3, 21 March 2018) of a law-review article; legal and technical argument on the pre-2026 EU text, not an empirical study.

items.title: How do people feel about AI? 2025 survey: Key findings
items.publisher: Ada Lovelace Institute and The Alan Turing Institute
items.locator: Key findings, paragraph on laws, regulation and appeal procedures; methodology page for the sample
items.quote: along with 61% who felt getting information on how AI systems made decisions about them would increase their comfort levels
items.why: UK evidence on the link between being told and trust: 65% said appeal procedures, and 61% said information on how a decision about them was made, would make them more comfortable with AI. Nationally representative sample of 3,513 people, fieldwork 25 October to 24 November 2024. Stated attitudes, not observed behaviour; institute report, not peer reviewed.
